sentences: IAMAI reads your Microsoft 365 tenant and tells you who each change locks out, what order to make them in, and what to watch afterwards.

Start from a maintained policy set, or upload a package.
Who could pass MFA today, who needs a hand, and who is blocked right now: by name.

A Global Administrator or Global Reader account.
Entra ID P1 for sign-in records.

The Conditional Access configuration: to compare it with the baseline.

Recent interactive sign-in records: to check that MFA works before anything is enforced.
No changes to the tenant: the app holds read-only permissions only.
No tenant data is sent anywhere on its own.
There is no server, no analytics and no telemetry.
What you export moves when you choose it: saving a plan or a CSV, copying a prompt, printing, or emailing feedback.
No account required with anyone.
The source is public, so every claim above can be checked.
Predicted impact, confirmed in report-only.

repository
how to make one
summaries: Technical details
sentences: Picks the target policy set the rollout plan aims for.
A baseline is a set of Conditional Access policies somebody has already worked out and maintains: what to require, of whom, and in what order.
IAMAI compares this tenant against one and builds the plan from the difference, so the target is a published policy set rather than an opinion.
Jon Hope — Defense in Depth CA baseline by Jon Hope, Microsoft MVP in identity and access · repository
version ceccdc2
A defence-in-depth Conditional Access policy set covering identity, device, session, and workload protections, maintained as importable Graph policy JSON.
Bring a tenant to a layered, exclusion-aware Conditional Access posture without lockouts, starting from MFA for everyone and building up to device and session controls.
155 files, 1 usable policy · targets Entra ID P1, Entra ID P2

sentences: Explains the naming convention behind every name IAMAI proposes, and how it reads the one this tenant already uses.
A Conditional Access policy name is the only thing an admin sees in a list of forty.
A good one answers three questions without opening it: who it applies to, what it does, and whether it is on purpose.
The convention below is a common one, not the only one.
What matters is that a tenant picks one and holds to it.
Prefix.
Groups policies that belong to one set, so they sort together and a stranger can tell yours from Microsoft’s.
Scope.
Who it applies to: Global, Admins, Guests, or a persona.
Action.
Block, Require, Grant, or Session.
Target.
The thing being protected or restricted.
